# Work finish

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Takes an approved item through the pull request, merge, deployment, and requirements update to Done, or cancels it; it never marks Done without the owner's approval and never runs a production deploy. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Check the result approval is recorded. Not recorded: show the result, the gaps, and the evidence, and ask. "Ship it" or "mark it done" after he saw the result counts: save his words first, then record it (`references/approvals.md`, section 4). Each sub-item needs its own.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Result approved; work-finish continues.'`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
2. Repository work: commit the item's files by name on its branch, push it, open the pull request, and set the stage (`references/closing.md`, section 2; `references/git-rules.md` before any Git write).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 12-pr-and-push`
3. Merge through `merge-and-clean-up` only with the owner's yes to this merge, or a standing merge instruction with an independent check on the exact head (`references/closing.md`, section 3). No remote: the local merge (`references/closing.md`, section 4), then this note.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'No remote: merged locally into <default branch>.' --effect 'No pull request; no deployment.'`
4. Deployment, when the item needs one (`references/closing.md`, section 5). Production deploys and production data loads are the owner's to run. Salesforce: a sandbox validate runs; a sandbox deploy needs his yes for that deploy, and in Codex he runs every sandbox deploy and sandbox data change himself, so give him the exact command with its `-o <sandbox>`. Run each `sf` command directly, never from a script.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 13-deployment`
5. Requirements baseline: copy only delivered and approved behavior into the area's file in `requirements/`, update `system-guide/` when the structure changed, and save both with `publish-docs` (`references/closing.md`, section 6).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 14-spec-update`
6. Sub-items: list the open ones; each is finished, cancelled, or moved on its own (`references/closing.md`, section 7).
   `toolkit work list --tree`
7. Memory: at most one `event` record through `memory-save`, only when the episode will matter later.
8. Before Done, run the Done checklist in `references/approvals.md`, section 5, with the Overview and Roadmap updates and the leftover worktrees in `references/closing.md`, sections 9 and 10. Take the item off the current focus now, before the finish command, so the backup it makes holds the new focus (`references/current-focus.md`); if the finish refuses, put the item back. Then mark it Done. The command also backs up the tracker and memory: read its backup line. "No backup folder is set" or a line with "failed" goes to the owner as a question (`references/closing.md`, section 10).
   `toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>'`
9. Say whether the work reached the default branch. End with the one question (the merge, the deploy, a leftover branch, the backup folder) or "Tell me the next thing to build."
10. Cancel instead: the owner's words are the reason; ask about each open sub-item first (`references/approvals.md`, section 6).
    `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Never mark Done without a recorded result approval or the owner's quoted words. The CLI needs `--by`, and `--quote` when no result approval is recorded.
- Never mark Done while the item's changes, or its `requirements/` and `system-guide/` updates, are uncommitted.
- A result approval never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing. Each needs the owner's yes or a standing instruction recorded in `DECISIONS.md`.
- A standing merge instruction needs an `acceptance-checker` that did not build the change to find no blocking issue on that exact head. Without that check, ask the owner.
- Agents never run a production deploy or a production data load. Hand the owner the exact command and what to check afterwards; record his report in a history note.
- In Codex, every Git write needs the owner's approval and escalated permissions (`references/git-rules.md`). No remote: never run `git fetch` or `git push`.
- No AI credit in commits, pull requests, or release notes. The pull request description goes through `unslop`.
- Stages that do not apply are skipped, each with one history note saying so.
- Leave the folder or card where it is. Moving or archiving is `work-organize`'s, on the owner's request.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Close the issue as completed, or as not planned for a cancel (`references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`).

## Agents

- `acceptance-checker` (`references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`): the independent check of the exact head before a merge under a standing merge instruction. Brief it as `work-check` does and name the commit (`references/helpers.md`).
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Give the full text of this skill's `references/agent-<name>.md`, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran. Without an independent check, a standing merge instruction does not apply: ask the owner.

# The current focus

Purpose: the format of the current focus, when to change it, and the exact
read-change-save sequence, in every memory backend.

## Contents

- What the focus is for
- The format
- What goes in each section
- When to check it
- Read, change, save
- A new project's focus
- Examples
- Checklist for a focus save

## What the focus is for

The current focus is the first thing the next session reads: the session
briefing includes it. It says what is happening now and where the next
session starts. It never repeats the tracker: a work item's status, tasks,
and history stay in the work item.

| Backend | Where the focus lives |
| --- | --- |
| Built-in | `.memory/CURRENT_FOCUS.md` in the main checkout |
| Hindsight | The document `focus` in the project's bank |
| Notion | The "Current focus" page under the project's page |

The same commands read and save it in every backend. Never edit the file or
the page by hand.

## The format

The model's format: a `# Current focus` title line, a `Last updated:` line,
then exactly four `##` sections in this order, under 50 lines in total.

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: <YYYY-MM-DD>, <source>, <person or agent>

## Now

## Waiting on the owner

## Untracked to-dos

## Next session starts with
```

What the command enforces:

- It refuses a focus that lacks one of the four sections, has another
  section, or is over 50 lines (exit code 2, nothing saved).
- It adds the title line or the `Last updated:` line when either is missing,
  and sets an older date to today. It cannot know the source or who wrote
  it, so write the line yourself.

## What goes in each section

- **Last updated:** the date, the source (for example `handoff`,
  `work-finish`, `chat`), and who wrote it (a person, or `agent`). Change it
  on every save.
- **Now:** the current outcome or area, with work item ids and titles only,
  for example `- WI-012 CSV export`. Never a status or a stage: the tracker
  holds those.
- **Waiting on the owner:** a decision or action only the owner can take
  that has no work item: what it is, who needs it, and when to check again.
  Work items that wait on him are listed by `toolkit work decisions`, not
  here. A setup step (trust the hooks in Codex, sign in to Notion with
  `ntn login`) stays only while `toolkit doctor` still reports it.
- **Untracked to-dos:** things the owner asked for that have no work item.
  When one becomes a work item, replace the line with the item's id under
  Now.
- **Next session starts with:** one entry: where to resume, what to read,
  and the next action. It is replaced at each handoff, not added to.
- Write "None." in a section with nothing in it.
- Keep it under 50 lines by replacing stale lines, never by appending. Never
  drop an owner to-do that is still open only to meet the limit.

## When to check it

Check the focus before the reply ends when:

- a work item's stage changes, or its next step changes to something the
  focus does not say. Check two things:
  1. Now lists the item (id and title). Add it when it is missing; take it
     off when the item is Done or Cancelled. For Done, take it off just
     before `toolkit work finish`, which backs up the focus as it is then.
  2. Next session starts with does not name a step that is done or no longer
     next. Replace that line with the item's real next step, in one line that
     points at the item, for example "Continue WI-012 from its Resume here:
     build P1."
- the owner asks for something with no work item (add it under Untracked
  to-dos), or a decision only he can make has no work item (Waiting on the
  owner).
- `toolkit doctor` no longer reports a setup step listed under Waiting on the
  owner (drop it).
- a session hands off (replace the one entry under Next session starts
  with).

Skip the save when nothing in the focus is wrong. Leave every line you are
not changing exactly as it is.

## Read, change, save

1. Read it with its version. The output has `text` and `version`:

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --json
   ```

2. Change only the lines that need it, in the whole text, and update the
   `Last updated:` line.
3. Save the whole text with the version you read.
   Claude Code: `<file>` is `-`, with the text on standard input after a
   quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`), then a line holding only `EOF`.

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>
   ```

   Codex: give the text in single quotes instead (newlines are kept), or
   use a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder and delete it after the save.
   Write an apostrophe as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the
   text. Never `'\''` in Codex: the project's command rule does not match
   that form, so the command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can
   drop the backslash.

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
   ```

4. Exit code 2 with "changed since it was read" means another session saved
   the focus after you read it. Read it again, make your change in the new
   text, and save with the new version. Never save without `--expect`: that
   would silently drop the other session's change.
5. No focus yet (`version` is null): save with `--expect absent`, in the full
   format above.
6. Read it back:

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus
   ```

## A new project's focus

A new project's focus still holds the model's setup text: a fill-in guide
comment under the title (`<!-- Fill-in guide: ... -->`) and an
`<angle-bracket>` prompt in every section. At the first save:

- remove the fill-in guide comment;
- replace each prompt with real content, or with "None." when there is none;
- never leave an angle-bracket prompt in a saved focus.

## Examples

A full focus:

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: 2026-09-26, handoff, agent

## Now

- WI-012 CSV export
- WI-015 Large exports (sub-item of WI-012)

## Waiting on the owner

- Pick a hosting provider before the first deploy (no work item yet); check again 2026-10-01.

## Untracked to-dos

- Email the client about the October demo.

## Next session starts with

- 2026-09-26 17:40 UTC | CSV export: continue WI-012 from its Resume here. Goal: exports finish under 10 seconds.
```

The handoff entry with a work item is a pointer only:
`<UTC date and time> | <topic>: continue <WI-id> from its Resume here. Goal: <one line>.`

With no work item, the entry is a short note: the goal or topic, where work
stopped, the first next action, limits on what may be done without the
owner, and open questions. Do not create a work item only to hold it.

## Checklist for a focus save

- [ ] Read with `--json`; you have the version.
- [ ] The `# Current focus` title and the `Last updated:` line (date,
      source, who) are there.
- [ ] Four sections, in order; "None." in each empty one.
- [ ] Work item ids and titles only; no status or stage.
- [ ] No angle-bracket prompt and no fill-in guide comment left.
- [ ] Under 50 lines; no open owner to-do dropped.
- [ ] Saved with `--expect`; read back.

# Work item and design format

What a work item and its design hold, their exact section names, and how to
change them with `toolkit work` commands without losing text.

## Contents

1. Where the record and the design live
2. Header fields
3. Sections of `WORK-ITEM.md`
4. Sections of `DESIGN.md`
5. Finding an item's file
6. Changing one section
7. Adding a table row
8. Editing a record directly
9. Titles
10. Generated files
11. Examples

## 1. Where the record and the design live

Every tracker uses the same body and the same design shape. Only the place
differs.

| Tracker | Work item | Design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local | `WORK-ITEM.md` in the item's folder under `.work-items/` | `DESIGN.md` beside it |
| Notion | The item's page in the project's Work Items database | The item's "Solution Design" child page |
| GitHub Issues | The issue body | One issue comment whose first line is `## Solution design` |
| Jira | The issue description | One comment whose first line is "Solution design" |

An item has one design home. Never make a separate design folder or a second
design file.

## 2. Header fields

The header (frontmatter locally, properties in Notion) holds these fields.
Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

| Field | Values | Changed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `WI-001` (the project's prefix and a number) | `toolkit work new`; never reused |
| `title` | The owner's words for the request | `toolkit work set <id> --title` |
| `type` | `discovery`, `solution-design`, `build`, `data-load`, `repository-maintenance`, `research`, `task`, `bug`, `enhancement`, or another lower-case word | `toolkit work set <id> --type` |
| `stage` | `01-discovery` to `14-spec-update` | `toolkit work set <id> --stage`, `approve`, `finish`, `cancel` |
| `status` | Backlog, Ready, In Progress, In Review, Done, Cancelled | Follows the stage; Done and Cancelled only through `finish` and `cancel` |
| `parent` | An item id or `none` | `toolkit work new --parent`, `toolkit work move` |
| `waiting_on` | `owner`, `agent`, `external: <who>`, `none` | `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on` |
| `priority` | `urgent`, `high`, `medium`, `low` | `toolkit work set <id> --priority` |
| `delivery` | `agent-led`, `owner-led`, `not-offered` | `toolkit work set <id> --delivery` |
| `requirements_approved` | `YYYY-MM-DD by <name>` or `no` | `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements` |
| `design` | `proposed`, `approved`, `superseded`, `none` | `toolkit work design`, `toolkit work approve <id> --design` |
| `result_approved` | `YYYY-MM-DD by <name>` or `no` | `toolkit work approve <id> --result`, `toolkit work finish --quote` |
| `updated` | `YYYY-MM-DD` | Every `toolkit work` write |

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stage labels, the statuses, and the types.
Blocked is not a status: an item that cannot move has `waiting_on` set and its
Overview Blockers line filled.

## 3. Sections of `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` takes. A `###` subsection can be named on
its own, for example `--section 'Agreed goal'`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | The phase table: Phase (`P1 — <name>`), Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | One `### P1 — <name>` heading per phase, with checkbox tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: Date, Change or decision, Effect on the work (newest first) |
| `Open Questions` | Rows: ID (`Q-01`), Question, Affects, Status, Decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status and Finalization rule, then the subsections below |
| `Starting request` | The owner's own words for the request |
| `Agreed goal` | The outcome the owner agreed the item delivers |
| `Active requirements` | One `#### R-01 — <name>` block per requirement |
| `Acceptance` | The numbered list of what makes the whole item acceptable |
| `Notes` | The subsections below |
| `Decisions and context` | Context the next session needs that is not a requirement |
| `Resume here` | Where the next session picks up |
| `Solution options and considerations` | Build ideas, linked to an `R-xx`; never requirements |

The `R-xx` block fields are Status (Refining, Finalized, Superseded), Applies
to, Required behavior, Boundaries and exceptions, Acceptance check, Decision
record, and Open questions. Each field starts its own line.

In the local and Notion trackers, the requirements approval command sets the
Requirements "Overall status" line: never write that line by hand there.
GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so after the owner's yes the
agent writes Finalized there itself (`tracker-github.md` or `tracker-jira.md`,
"The `toolkit work` steps").

## 4. Sections of `DESIGN.md`

The CLI writes the design's header fields: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what is left to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C), each with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage, Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow; Components and responsibilities; Data, access, and integration details; Edge cases and failure behavior; Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep every heading exactly as the template has it, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`. In the local and Notion trackers, never write "Approved"
in the Design status line: a save replaces that line with the stored status,
and only `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>` approves a design.
GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so after the owner's yes the
agent writes Approved there itself (`tracker-github.md` or `tracker-jira.md`).

## 5. Finding an item's file

Never build a path by hand. The owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

```text
toolkit work show <id> --path
```

`toolkit work show <id>` also prints the item's stage, who it waits on, the
skill that continues it, its parent and sub-items, its design (or the
parent's approved design it inherits), and the worktree branch and folder to
use.

## 6. Changing one section

1. Read the section. The output is the whole section as it stands.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section '<heading>'`
2. Change only what needs to change. Keep the rest word for word.
3. Leave out the section's fill-in guide comment (`<!-- ... -->`) once the
   section holds real content.
4. Write the whole section back. `<file>` is `-` in Claude Code, with the text
   on standard input; in Codex use `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new
   `mktemp -d` folder (`toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section '<heading>' --set-file <file>`
5. Read it back. An exit code of `0` is not proof by itself.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section '<heading>'`

To remove the template's fill-in guide above Overview:

```text
toolkit work edit <id> --remove-guide
```

## 7. Adding a table row

Add one row to Open Questions or Recent History with `--append-row` and the
full Markdown row in single quotes.

A new question takes the next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions
section first and add one to the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is
none). "Decision needed from" is `owner` for the owner, or a person or role.

```text
toolkit work show <id> --section 'Open Questions'
toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| Q-03 | Should the export include archived rows? | R-02 | Open | owner |'
```

A history row is added with its own command, which writes the date:

```text
toolkit work history <id> --note '<what happened>' --effect '<what it changes>'
```

To answer a question, rewrite its row in the whole Open Questions section:
the answer, the date, and status Answered. An approve command or a
`--delivery` answer marks the rows that asked for it Answered by itself and
prints "Marked Q-xx Answered"; do not edit those rows again.

  keeps the CLI's record of what it wrote.
- A local record's body text may also be changed with the file edit tool. The
  post-tool hook checks the record after the edit.
- Never change the header fields with a file edit, and never create a record
  with one. The pre-tool hook refuses both, because they would skip the
  approval gates.
- Never write a record from the shell: no `cat >`, `tee`, `sed -i`, `cp`, and

- A Notion item changes only through `toolkit work` commands. Never write its

- A new item's title uses the owner's own words for the request. When you
  shorten them, say the title in one line in the reply ("I started WI-003,

  retitle quietly.

  used.

# Running `toolkit` commands

Purpose: how to run a `toolkit` command in Claude Code and in Codex, how to
pass text in one, and what each exit code means. Every skill that runs a
`toolkit` command follows this file.

## Contents

- Running toolkit commands
- Text in a command
- Exit codes
- Reporting a save
- Reading output and updating what you read
- Right and wrong examples

## Running toolkit commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command,
  in both hosts. Do not join it to another command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe,
  and do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a loop, or a script. This holds for read
  commands too: `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two
  commands, run one after the other.
- Why, in Codex: the project's command rule (`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules`)
  runs a `toolkit` command outside the sandbox only when it is the whole
  command. A `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion, the
  local Hindsight server, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and
  `.memory/` from a worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong
  cause.
- The one thing a Claude Code command may carry is its own text on standard
  input (`--set-file -` with a quoted heredoc; "Text in a command", below).
- Five commands ask the owner first, in both hosts, because they are hard or
  impossible to undo: `toolkit machine-setup`, `toolkit memory delete`,
  `toolkit memory import`, `toolkit import`, and
  `toolkit hindsight service install` or `start`. Get his yes in the reply
  before you run one. The host then asks him to confirm the command (Claude
  Code: a permission prompt; Codex: an approval). That prompt is expected, not
  an error.
- When the host refuses one of the five without asking him (Codex with
  approvals off: "approval required by policy, but AskForApproval is set to
  Never"), say that the cause is that approval setting, show him the exact
  command to run himself in a terminal, and wait. Do nothing in its place
  that he did not ask for: a refused delete is not a retire.
- In Codex, run each of those five alone, with `sandbox_permissions` set to
  `require_escalated` and a one-line reason. The approval alone keeps the
  command inside the sandbox, where it fails: `toolkit memory delete` cannot
  reach Hindsight or Notion, `toolkit machine-setup` cannot write `~/.codex`
  or `~/.local/bin`, `toolkit hindsight service install` cannot write
  `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, and `toolkit import` from a worktree cannot write
  the main checkout.
- Write `--json` and `--host` after the command words
  (`toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved --json`). The toolkit refuses
  those five commands when a flag comes first, because the ask-first rules
  would not match them.
- Never change a work item or a memory record with a script or a shell write
  (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`, `tee`, `cp`). Use the `toolkit` command
  that owns it. The hooks refuse the shell write, so it only wastes a step.
- `toolkit help <command>` prints every option of one command.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still reports success. So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Never use double quotes for text.
- **An apostrophe inside single quotes:**
  - Claude Code: write it as `'\''`, for example
    `--note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`.
  - Codex: write it as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the text.
    Never `'\''` in Codex: the command rule does not match that form, so the
    command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can drop the
    backslash, which leaves a quote that is never closed.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere.
  Claude Code refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary file there
  could never be deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line
  holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --set-file - <<'EOF'
  <the whole section text>
  EOF
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text:
  1. Make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d`. Its name is
     unique, so two sessions or two projects never share a file.
  2. Write the file in it with the file edit tool (`apply_patch`).
  3. Run the `toolkit` command alone, with the file's full path.
  4. Delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds
     (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner anything.

  Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
  ```

- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`. Every
  project starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this
  item.
- Never leave a draft file inside `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. A second
  `DESIGN.md`-shaped file there confuses the design lookup, and a stray note
  in `.memory/` is read as a memory.

## Exit codes

`toolkit help work` prints them as: "0 ok, 1 error, 2 validation failure or a
refused gate, 3 not supported for this tracker, 4 not a toolkit project."
`toolkit help memory` uses the same numbers: "1 error or not found, 2 refused
(a rule or a stale --expect), 3 not supported by this backend".

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | Done. | Read back what you wrote before you report it as saved ("Reporting a save", below). A "Note:" line in the output still needs action: report it to the owner, or do what it says. |
| `1` | Error, or the record was not found. | Read the message. It names the cause and usually the fix. Do not run the same command again unchanged. |
| `2` | Validation failure, a refused gate, or a stale `--expect`. | Fix what the message names and run the command again. A refused gate means an approval is missing: ask the owner for it. Never work around a refusal. |
| `3` | Not supported for this tracker or memory backend. | For a GitHub or Jira tracker, the message prints the path of the written instructions for that tracker. Follow them to make the same change on the issue. |
| `4` | Not a Toolkit V2 project. | Skip every work item and memory step and say so in one line. To set the project up, open the `project-setup` skill. |

`toolkit: command not found` means this computer cannot reach the command.
The `project-setup` skill fixes that.

## Reporting a save

- Save each settled answer before moving on, then read it back. A command
  that exits `0` is not proof by itself.
- A write failed: lead the reply with "Not saved". Name what was not saved
  and where it should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- "Saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first part that differs. Lead the
  reply with "Saved but not verified", say which part, and read the record
  back to judge it.

## Reading output and updating what you read

- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field, for example
  a record's `version`.
- `--expect <version>` tells the command which version of a record you read.
  The command refuses the save (exit `2`) when the record changed since then,
  so you never overwrite a newer edit. Read it again, merge, and save with the
  new version. `toolkit memory focus`, `toolkit memory glossary`, and
  `toolkit memory save` take it. `--expect absent` says it must not exist
  yet: a new record, or a project with no focus yet.

## Right and wrong examples

1. Two reads.
   - Wrong: `toolkit work list && toolkit work show WI-004`
   - Right: `toolkit work list`, then, as a second command,
     `toolkit work show WI-004`.
2. A history note that quotes the owner, with an apostrophe in his words.
   - Wrong: ``toolkit work history WI-004 --note "Owner said: it's ready, `ship it`"``
     (double quotes: the shell runs the words between the backticks as a
     command and saves its output in their place).
   - Right in Claude Code:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`
   - Right in Codex:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it’s ready, ship it"'`
   - The prefix is `Owner said:`, which has no apostrophe to escape.
3. Section text in Codex.
   - Wrong: `cat > /tmp/overview.md <<'EOF' ... EOF && toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --set-file /tmp/overview.md`
     (one shell command, a heredoc, and a fixed file name).
   - Right: `toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'`
4. A change to a work item's header.
   - Wrong: `sed -i '' 's/^stage: .*/stage: 04-solution-design/' .work-items/WI-004/WORK-ITEM.md`
   - Right: `toolkit work set WI-004 --stage 04-solution-design --note '<why>'`
5. Toolkit commands from a script.
   - Wrong: `for id in WI-001 WI-002; do toolkit work show $id; done`
   - Right: `toolkit work show WI-001`, then `toolkit work show WI-002`, each
     as its own command.

# Closing a work item

The detail behind each `work-finish` step: the pull request and merge, a
merge with no remote, deployment, the requirements baseline, sub-items,
memory, leftover worktrees, Done, and cancel.

## Contents

1. Before anything ships
2. Commit, push, and the pull request (stage 12)
3. Merging
4. No remote: the local merge
5. Deployment (stage 13)
6. Requirements baseline (stage 14)
7. Sub-items
8. Memory and the current focus
9. Leftover worktrees and branches
10. Done
11. Cancel

## 1. Before anything ships

- The result approval is recorded (`toolkit work show <id>` shows
  `result_approved`), or the owner said "ship it" or "mark it done" after he
  saw the result, the gaps, and the evidence. Record that with his words
  (`approvals.md`, "Result approval").
- Never describe an unverified result as complete.
- Done means the owner accepted the result. Cancelled means the work stopped
  without it.
- Stages that do not apply are skipped. Work with no repository change has no
  pull request; work with no deployment has no deployment stage. A skipped
  stage gets one history note saying so, so `toolkit work finish` has a
  record of it.

## 2. Commit, push, and the pull request (stage 12)

- Commit the item's files on its branch, staged by name
  (`claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, for example `claude/wi-007-csv-export`).
  No `Co-Authored-By` line naming an AI and no "Generated with" line.
- Push the branch. Never force-push.
- Write the pull request title and description in plain words: what changed,
  why, how it was checked, and the item id. Run the description through the
  `unslop` skill, because other people read it. No line crediting an AI.
- Set the stage:
  `toolkit work set <id> --stage 12-pr-and-push`
- In Codex, every Git write here needs the owner's approval and escalated
  permissions (`git-rules.md`).

## 3. Merging

Merge only through `merge-and-clean-up`, and only when one of these holds:

- the owner said yes to this merge; or
- a standing merge instruction applies (`approvals.md`, "Standing merge
  instruction"): it is recorded in `DECISIONS.md`, an `acceptance-checker`
  that did not build the change found no blocking issue on that exact head
  commit, and every check passes.

A work item that says its merge needs the owner's approval overrides a
standing instruction. Without an independent check, the standing instruction
does not apply: ask the owner.

A merge that stops on a conflict: resolve it and commit with a message you
write (`git commit -m 'Merge <branch>: <what it brings>'`). Never
`git commit --no-edit`: it keeps Git's "# Conflicts:" lines in the message.

## 4. No remote: the local merge

`git remote` prints nothing: the project has no remote. There is no push and
no pull request, and `git fetch` is never run.

- [ ] The same approval as a merge applies (section 3).
- [ ] The merge-safety check (`git-rules.md`, "The merge-safety check"):
      list the files the merge brings in, and the primary checkout's
      uncommitted files. A file in both lists: stop, name exactly those
      files, and let the owner decide.
      `git diff --name-only <default branch>...<branch>`
      `git -C <primary checkout> status --porcelain`
- [ ] In the main checkout, on the default branch:
      `git merge --ff-only <branch>`
- [ ] The fast-forward fails when the default branch moved on after the
      item's branch was made (for example another item's local merge). Then,
      in the item's worktree: `git merge <default branch>`, run the item's
      checks again (under a standing merge instruction the
      `acceptance-checker` checks the new head), run the merge-safety check
      again, and run the fast-forward again.
- [ ] Set the stage anyway and record it, with the real name of the default
      branch in the note:
      `toolkit work set <id> --stage 12-pr-and-push`
      `toolkit work history <id> --note 'No remote: merged locally into <default branch>.' --effect 'No pull request; no deployment.'`

## 5. Deployment (stage 13)

Only when the result must be put somewhere beyond the default branch.

`toolkit work set <id> --stage 13-deployment`

Salesforce projects, in order:

- [ ] `sf-component-tracker` is current, and the item's folder
      `delivery/deployment/<work-item-id>-<short-name>/` holds its
      `package.xml`, `destructiveChanges.xml` when something is removed,
      `manual-steps.md`, and `DEPLOYMENT-RECORD.md`.
- [ ] `sf-deploy-check` finds nothing that would ship too early.
- [ ] A validate against the sandbox. It needs no yes, in both hosts.
- [ ] A sandbox deploy, when the item needs one: in Claude Code, only after
      the owner's yes for that deploy, in this chat.
- [ ] In Codex, the owner runs every sandbox deploy and sandbox data change,
      including `sf apex run` against a sandbox. Hand him the exact command
      with its `-o <sandbox>`; do not run it yourself, even after his yes.
- [ ] Run each `sf` command directly, never from a script or file you wrote,
      so the guard sees it (`salesforce-org-safety.md`).
- [ ] A DevOps Center pipeline deploy (`sf project deploy pipeline start`,
      `quick`, `resume`, or `validate`) goes to the owner: the command does
      not name the org it reaches, and that org can be production.
- [ ] A production deploy is handed to the owner: the exact command, what it
      deploys, and what to check afterwards. Agents never run it.
- [ ] Production data changes go through `sf-data-change`, which builds the
      owner's package. The owner runs it.
- [ ] A release of several items uses a copy of
      `delivery/deployment/release-cutover-template/`.

Record the owner's report of the deploy in a history note.

## 6. Requirements baseline (stage 14)

`toolkit work set <id> --stage 14-spec-update`

- The work item held the proposed requirements while the work was in
  progress. After delivery and approval, copy the delivered rules into the
  area's file in `requirements/`. Read `requirements/AGENTS.md` first.
- Each business area has one folder holding one maintained file. A new area:
  copy `requirements/system-area-template/` to a folder named for the area,
  then name the copied `AREA-TEMPLATE.md` for the area, for example
  `requirements/billing/BILLING.md`. Fill it as its guide says and delete the
  guide. Leave `system-area-template/` unchanged for the next area.
- Rules that apply across areas go in `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md`.
- Copy only behavior that was delivered and approved. Behavior that was
  approved but not delivered is never written as shipped.
- Link the work item id from the area file when it explains a requirement,
  and add a line to its Change history. Do not copy task history there.
- When the change altered the verified structure of the system, also update
  the area's file in `system-guide/` (a new area is a copy of
  `system-guide/AREA-TEMPLATE.md` named for the area, for example
  `system-guide/billing.md`), with the observed facts and the date checked.
- Save these files with the `publish-docs` skill. It commits them from its own
  worktree and pushes them; with no remote it commits them on the default
  branch locally and says "No remote: committed locally".
- Confirm the item links to the requirements, decisions, and code that
  actually exist. Do not create missing documents only to complete a
  checklist.

## 7. Sub-items

- List the open sub-items before finishing a parent:
  `toolkit work list --tree`
- Each one is finished or cancelled on its own (with its own approval or
  reason), or moved when the owner asks (`work-organize`).
- A parent with open sub-items is finished only when the owner says so. Then
  `toolkit work finish` needs `--allow-open-sub-items` (without it the
  command refuses with exit code 2), and a history note quotes his words.
- Finishing a sub-item never finishes or approves its parent.
- Cancelling a parent: ask what happens to each open sub-item (cancel it,
  move it to the top level, or move it under another item). Never cancel
  them without asking.

## 8. Memory and the current focus

- At most one `event` memory through `memory-save`, only when the episode will
  matter later, for example a costly fix or a surprising platform limit.
- Take the item off the current focus "Now" list, replace a "Next session
  starts with" line that names it, and update the "Last updated" line
  (`current-focus.md`). The focus names work item ids, never their status.

## 9. Leftover worktrees and branches

- List the item's worktrees and branches, with its id prefix in lower case:
  `git worktree list`
  `git branch --list '*wi-007*'`
- Compare each with the default branch. Offer to remove the ones already
  delivered. Remove one only with the owner's yes, and never one that holds
  uncommitted work: `git worktree remove <folder>`, then
  `git branch -d <branch>`. A merged pull request's branch and worktree are
  removed by `merge-and-clean-up`.
- `git status` in the main checkout must show none of the item's files
  uncommitted.

## 10. Done

Run the Done checklist in `approvals.md` first. Then:

- Before the finish command: set each Roadmap phase the item completed to
  Done, and in Overview bring Related items up to date (which sub-items
  delivered what, and anything left to another item), set Current position to
  "Done on <date>: <evidence>", and set Blockers to "None.". A Done item that
  still names a deleted branch or a merge waiting for approval misleads the
  next reader.
- Also before the finish command: take the item off the current focus
  (section 8). The finish command makes the backup, and a focus changed after
  it is not in that backup until the next one. If the finish command
  refuses, put the item back on the focus.
- `toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>'`.
  The evidence names the test result, the pull request or commit, or what
  the owner saw. The command sets Next action to "None. Finished." and Notes >
  Resume here to "Finished on <date>. Nothing to resume.", and prints a note
  when stages 12 to 14 left no record or a Roadmap phase is not Done. Answer
  each note it prints.
- The finish command then backs up `.work-items/` and `.memory/` (and
  Hindsight memory) to the owner's backup folder, and prints one line about
  it. Read that line:
  - "No automatic backup: this project keeps its work items and memory
    outside this computer ...": a Notion tracker with Notion memory. Nothing
    is copied; say so in one line when the owner set a backup folder.
  - "Backed up ... to <folder>": say it in one line in the reply.
  - "No backup folder is set ...": ask the owner for a folder outside the
    project, as the one question of the reply. After his answer:
    `toolkit config set backup.dir <folder>` (`none` when he wants no
    backup).
  - A line with "failed" or "Tell the owner": tell him that line as it is.
    The item is still Done; only the backup is missing.
- Repository work: say whether the work reached the default branch.
- Leave the folder or card where it is. Moving or archiving happens only on
  the owner's request, through `work-organize`.
- End the reply with the one question for the owner (the merge, the deploy, a
  leftover branch, the backup folder), or the exact words that continue
  ("Tell me the next thing to build.").

## 11. Cancel

- `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`. The reason is his
  words, not a summary.
- Ask about each open sub-item first (section 7).
- Cancelling keeps the record. Nothing is deleted.

# Approvals and gates

The exact steps to ask for and record each owner approval, and what counts as
one. Run each checklist in order; one wrong or missing command leaves the
item in the wrong state.

## Contents

1. What counts as approval
2. Requirements approval
3. Design approval
4. Result approval
5. Done
6. Cancel
7. Delivery offer
8. Project-wide decision
9. Memory proposal
10. Sub-items and approvals
11. Standing merge instruction
12. When an approve command refuses

## 1. What counts as approval

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the gates and these rules. In short:

- Only the owner's explicit words count. Quote them in a history note.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer ("probably B"), silence, or a
  saved draft is not approval.
- An approval covers only what was shown. It never covers merge, deployment,
  spending, or publishing.
- An approval survives later stages. A stage alone does not prove approval:
  check the approval field (`toolkit work show <id>`).
- A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" answers only a yes-or-no question asked
  earlier in this conversation. When none was asked, or the waiting question
  is not a yes-or-no question, show the decision with its choices and your
  recommendation, and record nothing.
- After a yes, save his words first, in a history note that starts with
  `Owner said:`. Then run the gate's commands. A command that refuses then
  never loses his answer, and no later session asks him again.
- `--by <owner>` is his name exactly as `toolkit config get project.owner`
  prints it (for example "Mike Rihm", not "Mike"), so every approval names
  him the same way.
- When an approve command notes that the item's Overview still asks for
  that approval (Next action), write the step after the approval with the
  `toolkit work edit` command the note prints.

| The owner says | After this question | It is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Yes, approved." | "Do you approve these requirements?" | The requirements approval |
| "Go with B." | The design options with a recommendation | The choice and approval of Option B |
| "Looks good." | "Do you approve this result?" | The result approval |
| "Looks good." | "Shall I split WI-12 into these three sub-items?" | A yes to the split only, not a result approval |
| "ok" | Nothing was asked in this chat | Not an answer; ask what he wants |
| "Probably A, but let me think." | The design options | Not an answer; the design stays proposed |
| "Ship it." | He has seen the result, gaps, and evidence | The result approval (record it with his words) |

## 2. Requirements approval

Asked by `work-requirements`. `work-decide` records a later answer.

Before asking:

- [ ] The Agreed goal holds real text. The CLI refuses the approval while it
      still holds the template text.
- [ ] The spec check ran (`requirements-analyst`), and its findings were fixed
      or turned into questions.
- [ ] No Open Questions row linked to a requirement is still open. If one is,
      say which and ask it first.

Ask: show the Agreed goal, each requirement in one line, the Acceptance list,
and any open question. Then ask exactly "Do you approve these requirements?"
as the last line, and set the item waiting on the owner.

```text
toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner
```

After his yes, in this order:

- [ ] Save his words first, so no later session asks him again.
      `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Requirements approved.'`
- [ ] Set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and add who approved it and
      when to its Decision record, in one edit of `Active requirements`.
      `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Active requirements' --set-file <file>`
- [ ] Record the approval. It adds its own history row, marks the Open
      Questions rows that asked for it Answered, sets `waiting_on` to `none`,

# Git rules for Toolkit V2 skills

Purpose: the Git rules every Toolkit V2 skill follows when it makes a branch,
commits, merges, pushes, or removes a worktree, in Claude Code and in Codex.

## Contents

- Look before the first Git write
- Branch and worktree names for a work item
- Staging and committing
- No AI credit
- The Git-ignored toolkit folders
- A project with no remote
- The merge-safety check
- A merge that stops on a conflict
- Git writes in Codex
- Checklist: one commit
- Examples

## Look before the first Git write

Other sessions may work in the same repository at the same time. Before the
first Git write in a session, run each of these on its own:

```text
git worktree list
git status
git remote
```

- `git remote` prints nothing: the project has no remote. Read "A project
  with no remote" below before any fetch, pull, push, or pull request.
- An unknown worktree, a branch that moved, or a change this session did not
  make means another session is working. Do not change it. Tell the owner.
- The shared primary checkout is the first entry `git worktree list` prints.
  In it, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never commit, push, rebase, or delete another session's branch, and never
  commit its uncommitted changes, even when they look finished.

## Branch and worktree names for a work item

A work item's code work happens in its own worktree, on its own branch.

| Part | Form | Example for `WI-007`, "CSV export" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branch | `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` | `claude/wi-007-csv-export` |
| Worktree folder | `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` | `.claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export` |

- `<prefix>` is the item's own id prefix in lower case: `wi` for `WI-007`,
  `tv2` for `TV2-007`, `acme` for `ACME-007`.
- The session briefing and `merge-and-clean-up` find the item from the id in
  the branch name. A branch named `wi-001-<slug>` for item `TV2-001` is not
  linked to that item.
- Make both with one command:

  ```text
  git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export
  ```

- Build on the item's branch, never on the default branch.

## Staging and committing

- Stage each path by name. Never run `git add -A`, `git add .`, or
  `git commit -a`: in a shared checkout they take other sessions' files.
- Read the staged file list, then the full staged diff, before the commit.
  Unstage any file this session did not write.

  ```text
  git diff --cached --name-status
  git diff --cached
  ```

- Write a plain commit message that says what changed, in one line when one
  line is enough.

## No AI credit

Nothing committed or published names an AI as an author or a helper:

- no `Co-Authored-By:` line naming an AI (a line naming a real person is
  allowed);
- no "Generated with" line;
- no AI credit in a pull request title or description, a code comment, a file
  header, or release notes.

The pre-tool hook refuses a commit or pull request command that carries such
a line. When it refuses, change the wording. Never commit another way to get
past it.

## The Git-ignored toolkit folders

`.work-items/` and `.memory/` are Git-ignored and live in the main checkout.

- Never commit them, and never force them in with `git add -f`. The hook
  refuses it.
- Never run `git clean -x` or `git clean -X` in the main checkout. It deletes
  both folders, and Git cannot bring them back. The hook refuses it.
- They change only through `toolkit work` and `toolkit memory` commands.
- Their backup is automatic: `toolkit work finish` and the handoff copy them
  to the owner's backup folder (`toolkit handoff-backup` does the same on
  request). `toolkit export --to <folder>` makes a one-off copy.

## A project with no remote

`git remote` prints nothing.

- Never run `git fetch`, `git pull`, or `git push`. A fetch that fails or is
  refused is not a blocker: never report it as one, and never write it into a
  work item.
- There is no pull request. `work-finish` merges the item's branch into the
  default branch locally, after the same approval a pull request merge needs,
  from the main checkout:

  ```text
  git merge --ff-only claude/wi-007-csv-export
  ```

  Then it adds the history note "No remote: merged locally into
  <default branch>."
- The fast-forward fails when the default branch moved on after the item's
  branch was made (for example another item's local merge). Merge the default
  branch into the item's branch in the item's worktree (`git merge main`, with
  the real default branch name), run the item's checks again, then run the
  fast-forward again.
- Documents are committed on the local default branch. `publish-docs` does
  this by itself.
- `merge-and-clean-up`, `pull-latest`, and `reset-to-remote` have nothing to
  do. Say so in one line.

## The merge-safety check

Before any merge into the default branch, check that it cannot overwrite
another session's uncommitted work in the primary checkout. With a remote,
fetch first so the comparison uses the remote's default branch.

```text
git diff --name-only main...claude/wi-007-csv-export
git -C <primary checkout> status --porcelain
```

Use the real default branch name, and `origin/<default branch>` when there is
a remote. A file in both lists: stop, name exactly those files, and let the
owner decide whether to commit, stash, or wait. Never touch the primary
checkout's changes yourself.

## A merge that stops on a conflict

1. Read both sides of each conflicting file. When the right result is not
   clear from the two sides, stop and ask the owner.
2. Stage each resolved file by name.
3. Commit with a message you write:

   ```text
   git commit -m 'Merge main into claude/wi-007-csv-export: keep both export formats'
   ```

Never run `git commit --no-edit` after a conflict: it keeps Git's
"# Conflicts:" lines in the message.

## Git writes in Codex

Codex's sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only. Every command that writes `.git/`
fails inside it: `git add`, `commit`, `merge`, `fetch`, `pull`, `push`,
`switch`, `checkout`, `restore`, `rm`, `mv`, `stash`, `cherry-pick`,
`revert`, `rebase`, `reset`, `update-ref`, `git worktree add`, `remove`,
`move`, `prune`, and `repair`, and `git branch -d`, `-D`, `-m`, `-c`, and
`-f`. The project's
`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` makes Codex ask the owner before each one. A `gh`
call that needs the network is also refused inside the sandbox.

Reading commands (`git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`,
`git branch --list`, `git worktree list`) run inside the sandbox as usual.

For each Git write in Codex:

- [ ] Run the Git command alone, as its own command: not joined to another
      command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and not from a script.
- [ ] Say in one line what the command does, before Codex asks the owner.
- [ ] Ask for escalated permissions: set `sandbox_permissions` to
      `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason that says what the command
      does ("Create the worktree for WI-002 on its own branch."). An approval
      without escalation still runs the command inside the sandbox, where it
      fails on `.git/index.lock`.
- [ ] Codex refused it without asking ("approval required by policy", or
      "AskForApproval is set to Never"): this session cannot ask. Stop that
      step, show the owner the exact command, and ask him to approve it in an
      interactive session or run it in a terminal. Set the work item waiting
      on the owner. It is not an outside blocker.

Never work around a refusal: no nested `git clone` of the project, no copy of
`.git/`, no script that runs Git for you, and no building on the default
branch instead of the item's branch. The `publish-docs` script is not such a
script: it is that skill's own tool. Run it alone with escalated permissions,
like any other Git write.

## Checklist: one commit

```text
- [ ] In the right worktree, on the right branch (git branch --show-current)
- [ ] Each path staged by name
- [ ] Staged list read: only this session's files, no .work-items/ or .memory/
- [ ] Full staged diff read
- [ ] Plain message with no AI credit line
- [ ] Codex: each Git command run alone, with escalated permissions
```

## Examples

Right: stage by name, read the list, commit.

```text
git add src/export.js tests/export.test.js
git diff --cached --name-status
git commit -m 'Add CSV export for invoices'
```

Wrong: `git add -A && git commit -m 'wip'`. It stages other sessions' files,
and in Codex the joined command runs inside the sandbox and fails.

Wrong: a message whose last line is a `Co-Authored-By:` trailer naming an AI
model. The hook refuses it. Remove the line and commit again.

Right, no remote: after the owner approves the result and the merge,

```text
git merge --ff-only claude/wi-007-csv-export
```

run from the main checkout, then the history note "No remote: merged locally
into main."

Right, Codex: `git commit -m 'Add CSV export for invoices'` run alone, with
`sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated` and the reason "Commit the
CSV export files for WI-007 on its branch."

Purpose: the Git rules every Toolkit V2 skill follows when it makes a branch,
commits, merges, pushes, or removes a worktree, in Claude Code and in Codex.

## Contents

- Look before the first Git write
- Branch and worktree names for a work item

## Look before the first Git write

Other sessions may work in the same repository at the same time. Before the
first Git write in a session, run each of these on its own:

```text
git worktree list
git status
git remote
```

- `git remote` prints nothing: the project has no remote. Read "A project
  with no remote" below before any fetch, pull, push, or pull request.
- An unknown worktree, a branch that moved, or a change this session did not
  make means another session is working. Do not change it. Tell the owner.
- The shared primary checkout is the first entry `git worktree list` prints.
  In it, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never commit, push, rebase, or delete another session's branch, and never
  commit its uncommitted changes, even when they look finished.

## Branch and worktree names for a work item

A work item's code work happens in its own worktree, on its own branch.

| Part | Form | Example for `WI-007`, "CSV export" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branch | `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` | `claude/wi-007-csv-export` |
| Worktree folder | `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` | `.claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export` |

- `<prefix>` is the item's own id prefix in lower case: `wi` for `WI-007`,
  `tv2` for `TV2-007`, `acme` for `ACME-007`.
- The session briefing and `merge-and-clean-up` find the item from the id in
  the branch name. A branch named `wi-001-<slug>` for item `TV2-001` is not
  linked to that item.
- Make both with one command:

  ```text
  git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export
  ```

- Build on the item's branch, never on the default branch.

## Staging and committing

- Stage each path by name. Never run `git add -A`, `git add .`, or
  `git commit -a`: in a shared checkout they take other sessions' files.
- Read the staged file list, then the full staged diff, before the commit.
  Unstage any file this session did not write.

  ```text
  git diff --cached --name-status
  git diff --cached
  ```

- Write a plain commit message that says what changed, in one line when one
  line is enough.

## No AI credit

Nothing committed or published names an AI as an author or a helper:

- no `Co-Authored-By:` line naming an AI (a line naming a real person is
  allowed);
- no "Generated with" line;
- no AI credit in a pull request title or description, a code comment, a file
  header, or release notes.

The pre-tool hook refuses a commit or pull request command that carries such
a line. When it refuses, change the wording. Never commit another way to get
past it.

## The Git-ignored toolkit folders

`.work-items/` and `.memory/` are Git-ignored and live in the main checkout.

- Never commit them, and never force them in with `git add -f`. The hook
  refuses it.
- Never run `git clean -x` or `git clean -X` in the main checkout. It deletes
  both folders, and Git cannot bring them back. The hook refuses it.
- They change only through `toolkit work` and `toolkit memory` commands.
- Their backup is automatic: `toolkit work finish` and the handoff copy them
  to the owner's backup folder (`toolkit handoff-backup` does the same on
  request). `toolkit export --to <folder>` makes a one-off copy.

## A project with no remote

`git remote` prints nothing.

- Never run `git fetch`, `git pull`, or `git push`. A fetch that fails or is
  refused is not a blocker: never report it as one, and never write it into a
  work item.
- There is no pull request. `work-finish` merges the item's branch into the
  default branch locally, after the same approval a pull request merge needs,
  from the main checkout:

  ```text
  git merge --ff-only claude/wi-007-csv-export
  ```

  Then it adds the history note "No remote: merged locally into
  <default branch>."
- The fast-forward fails when the default branch moved on after the item's
  branch was made (for example another item's local merge). Merge the default
  branch into the item's branch in the item's worktree (`git merge main`, with
  the real default branch name), run the item's checks again, then run the
  fast-forward again.
- Documents are committed on the local default branch. `publish-docs` does
  this by itself.
- `merge-and-clean-up`, `pull-latest`, and `reset-to-remote` have nothing to
  do. Say so in one line.

## The merge-safety check

Before any merge into the default branch, check that it cannot overwrite
another session's uncommitted work in the primary checkout. With a remote,
fetch first so the comparison uses the remote's default branch.

```text
git diff --name-only main...claude/wi-007-csv-export
git -C <primary checkout> status --porcelain
```

Use the real default branch name, and `origin/<default branch>` when there is
a remote. A file in both lists: stop, name exactly those files, and let the
owner decide whether to commit, stash, or wait. Never touch the primary
checkout's changes yourself.

## A merge that stops on a conflict

1. Read both sides of each conflicting file. When the right result is not
   clear from the two sides, stop and ask the owner.
2. Stage each resolved file by name.
3. Commit with a message you write:

   ```text
   git commit -m 'Merge main into claude/wi-007-csv-export: keep both export formats'
   ```

Never run `git commit --no-edit` after a conflict: it keeps Git's
"# Conflicts:" lines in the message.

## Git writes in Codex

Codex's sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only. Every command that writes `.git/`
fails inside it: `git add`, `commit`, `merge`, `fetch`, `pull`, `push`,
`switch`, `checkout`, `restore`, `rm`, `mv`, `stash`, `cherry-pick`,
`revert`, `rebase`, `reset`, `update-ref`, `git worktree add`, `remove`,
`move`, `prune`, and `repair`, and `git branch -d`, `-D`, `-m`, `-c`, and
`-f`. The project's
`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` makes Codex ask the owner before each one. A `gh`
call that needs the network is also refused inside the sandbox.

Reading commands (`git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`,
`git branch --list`, `git worktree list`) run inside the sandbox as usual.

For each Git write in Codex:

- [ ] Run the Git command alone, as its own command: not joined to another
      command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and not from a script.
- [ ] Say in one line what the command does, before Codex asks the owner.
- [ ] Ask for escalated permissions: set `sandbox_permissions` to
      `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason that says what the command
      does ("Create the worktree for WI-002 on its own branch."). An approval
      without escalation still runs the command inside the sandbox, where it
      fails on `.git/index.lock`.
- [ ] Codex refused it without asking ("approval required by policy", or
      "AskForApproval is set to Never"): this session cannot ask. Stop that
      step, show the owner the exact command, and ask him to approve it in an
      interactive session or run it in a terminal. Set the work item waiting
      on the owner. It is not an outside blocker.

Never work around a refusal: no nested `git clone` of the project, no copy of
`.git/`, no script that runs Git for you, and no building on the default
branch instead of the item's branch. The `publish-docs` script is not such a
script: it is that skill's own tool. Run it alone with escalated permissions,
like any other Git write.

# The current focus

Purpose: the format of the current focus, when to change it, and the exact
read-change-save sequence, in every memory backend.

## Contents

- What the focus is for
- The format
- What goes in each section
- When to check it
- Read, change, save
- A new project's focus
- Examples
- Checklist for a focus save

## What the focus is for

The current focus is the first thing the next session reads: the session
briefing includes it. It says what is happening now and where the next
session starts. It never repeats the tracker: a work item's status, tasks,
and history stay in the work item.

| Backend | Where the focus lives |
| --- | --- |
| Built-in | `.memory/CURRENT_FOCUS.md` in the main checkout |
| Hindsight | The document `focus` in the project's bank |
| Notion | The "Current focus" page under the project's page |

The same commands read and save it in every backend. Never edit the file or
the page by hand.

## The format

The model's format: a `# Current focus` title line, a `Last updated:` line,
then exactly four `##` sections in this order, under 50 lines in total.

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: <YYYY-MM-DD>, <source>, <person or agent>

## Now

## Waiting on the owner

## Untracked to-dos

## Next session starts with
```

What the command enforces:

- It refuses a focus that lacks one of the four sections, has another
  section, or is over 50 lines (exit code 2, nothing saved).
- It adds the title line or the `Last updated:` line when either is missing,
  and sets an older date to today. It cannot know the source or who wrote
  it, so write the line yourself.

## What goes in each section

- **Last updated:** the date, the source (for example `handoff`,
  `work-finish`, `chat`), and who wrote it (a person, or `agent`). Change it
  on every save.
- **Now:** the current outcome or area, with work item ids and titles only,
  for example `- WI-012 CSV export`. Never a status or a stage: the tracker
  holds those.
- **Waiting on the owner:** a decision or action only the owner can take
  that has no work item: what it is, who needs it, and when to check again.
  Work items that wait on him are listed by `toolkit work decisions`, not
  here. A setup step (trust the hooks in Codex, sign in to Notion with
  `ntn login`) stays only while `toolkit doctor` still reports it.
- **Untracked to-dos:** things the owner asked for that have no work item.
  When one becomes a work item, replace the line with the item's id under
  Now.
- **Next session starts with:** one entry: where to resume, what to read,
  and the next action. It is replaced at each handoff, not added to.
- Write "None." in a section with nothing in it.
- Keep it under 50 lines by replacing stale lines, never by appending. Never
  drop an owner to-do that is still open only to meet the limit.

## When to check it

Check the focus before the reply ends when:

- a work item's stage changes, or its next step changes to something the
  focus does not say. Check two things:
  1. Now lists the item (id and title). Add it when it is missing; take it
     off when the item is Done or Cancelled. For Done, take it off just
     before `toolkit work finish`, which backs up the focus as it is then.
  2. Next session starts with does not name a step that is done or no longer
     next. Replace that line with the item's real next step, in one line that
     points at the item, for example "Continue WI-012 from its Resume here:
     build P1."
- the owner asks for something with no work item (add it under Untracked
  to-dos), or a decision only he can make has no work item (Waiting on the
  owner).

# Publish a documentation save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Save an agreed change to Git-tracked project documents straight to the default
branch, with no pull request (rule: `.claude/rules/publish-project-documents.md`).

1. **Confirm it is documentation in an allowed path**, not code, rules, skills,
   hooks, settings, `.memory/`, or `.work-items/` (list below).
2. **Start a save workspace** with the script in the `scripts/` folder beside
   this `SKILL.md`. It fetches the remote (with no remote, it uses the local
   default branch), makes a sparse worktree in `.claude/worktrees/` (beside
   the project when Git does not ignore it), and prints its path. Work there.

   ```text
   node <this skill's folder>/scripts/publish-docs.mjs start --branch <default-branch> -- <file> [more files]
   ```

3. **Make the edit there and stage the files by name.** Read the full staged
   diff. Add `DECISIONS.md` rows only with `toolkit decision add`, run there.
   After a change under `ai-external-knowledge/`, regenerate its index there
   ("Step 3 in detail") and stage `ai-external-knowledge/INDEX.md` too.
4. **Publish** from the project folder, naming the path `start` printed. It
   refuses other staged, unstaged, or untracked files and conflict markers;
   commits; pushes without force and checks the remote has the commit. No
   remote: it moves the local default branch forward. It stops, or the push
   is refused: open `references/recovery.md`.

   ```text
   node <this skill's folder>/scripts/publish-docs.mjs publish --workspace <save workspace path> --message '<plain commit message>'
   ```

5. **Report** the commit id and where it is (the remote, or "No remote:
   committed locally on <branch>."), remove the clean save workspace after
   the task's last publish (`git worktree remove <path>`), and end with the
   one question for the owner or the exact words that continue.

## Gotchas

- Codex keeps `.git/` read-only. The script's `start` and `publish`,
  `git add`, and `git worktree remove` each run alone, with
  `sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated` and a one-line reason.
  Refused without asking: show the owner the exact command and wait
  (`references/git-rules.md`, "Git writes in Codex").
- Stage with `git -C <save workspace path> add -- <file>` and publish with
  `--workspace`, from the project folder. In Claude Code a `cd` into the save
  workspace is fine when it is under `.claude/worktrees/`; a `cd` into a
  workspace beside the project needs the owner's approval each time, and
  `claude -p` refuses it.
- When `start` put the workspace beside the project (the project's
  `.gitignore` does not list `.claude/worktrees/`), it is outside the folder
  Codex may write to. Codex asks the owner before every file edit or copy
  there, and under `codex exec` it refuses them. In a `codex exec` run, stop
  after `start`, show the owner the workspace path and the edit, and ask him
  to run the save in an interactive session.
- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch` or
  `git push` yourself. The script skips both and commits on the local default
  branch.
- Saving requirements or a design does not approve them or their build.
- `publish` refuses conflict markers and whitespace errors, but not two
  trailing spaces at the end of a line: that is a Markdown line break the
  templates use. Leave them.
- `DECISIONS.md` rows and `ai-external-knowledge/INDEX.md` are written by
  `toolkit` commands, never by hand.
- An unpushed commit is unfinished. The save is done only when the remote has
  the commit, or, with no remote, when the local default branch has it.

## What counts as documentation

The project documents are the paths in the project's
`publish-project-documents.md` rule. The script accepts only these:
